problems.source_says: Codebook section 4 defines lab_rct as a randomized experiment with people in a supervised session. The session was supervised, but the chapter never says that anything about the participants' conditions was random. All 62 students used both GPT-4 tools, one per task, and the order was counterbalanced into two groups of 31. The chapter does not say how students were allocated to the two orders, and Fig. 2 splits the sample after 'Instructions' with no randomization step. Counterbalancing sets how many people take each order. It does not say who takes which order. The form's own assignment.randomized = not_stated and criterion 1 = unclear conflict with a randomized design code. Keep lab_rct only if the authors confirm random allocation to order. Until then no form-spec code fits cleanly: quasi_people needs a without-AI condition, so 'other' with a note is the closest value, as in the c135 challenge.
problems.quote: A counterbalanced design was used: half completed the first task with ChatGPT-4 and the second with Mr. Ranedeer, while the other half followed the reverse order.
problems.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 Procedure and Fig. 2; codebook section 4; form-spec design_class field note

confirmed.statement: The design is within person. Each of the 62 students did two Product Improvement Tasks, one with standard ChatGPT-4 and one with the personalized GPT-4 tutor Mr. Ranedeer. The chapter calls the design within-subject(s) five times.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 376), Abstract; PDF p. 2 (printed p. 377), Sect. 1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 2.4; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Fig. 2 caption; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 386), Sect. 6

confirmed.statement: Every participant used both tools, so the only thing that varies across people is the order of the two AI conditions. Half did Task 1 with ChatGPT-4 and Task 2 with Mr. Ranedeer, and half did the reverse. Fig. 2 shows two groups of 31: 15 undergraduates and 16 graduates took the standard tool first, and 17 undergraduates and 14 graduates took the personalized tool first. These add up to the 32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students in Sect. 3.1. The form's assignment quote is verbatim and its locator is right. unit within_person_order and structure crossover fit this two-sequence design.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 and Fig. 2; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1

confirmed.statement: The chapter never says that the order, or the allocation of students to the two order groups, was random (checks a and e fail for lack of text). The only 'random' in the PDF text layer is the order in which raters saw the solutions. Fig. 2, rendered at high resolution, has no randomization step or wording, and no other figure mentions allocation. So randomized = not_stated, n_randomized = null, and criterion 1 = unclear are right.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 382), Sect. 3.4.1 ('Solutions were presented in randomized order'); PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 and Fig. 2; full-text search of PDF pp. 1-13

confirmed.statement: What was assigned is a generative-AI tool for the participant's own work (check b). Participants wrote three solutions in a document workspace beside the chat, 'using the assigned GAI tool', and two raters blind to condition scored those solutions. No condition differs only in whose output is evaluated.
confirmed.locator: PDF pp. 6-7 (printed pp. 381-382), Sect. 3.4.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 ('performed the task via the OpenAI web interface'); PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Fig. 3

confirmed.statement: Both tools are generative AI (check c). Both are built on OpenAI's GPT-4 and answer student prompts in natural language. Mr. Ranedeer is a GPT-4 tutor customized on OpenAI's 'Explore GPTs' platform and implemented via prompt engineering. Both arms are correctly coded generative_ai.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 380), Sect. 3.2.1; PDF p. 1 (printed p. 376), Abstract

confirmed.statement: The comparison arm matches the form (check d). The control is standard ChatGPT-4, another configuration of the same GPT-4 model, and the chapter has no no-AI arm. The chapter tests the personalized tutor against standard GAI (RQ1), so ai_design with treatment Mr. Ranedeer and control standard ChatGPT-4 follows codebook section 5.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 380), Sect. 3.2.1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 2.4 (RQ1); codebook section 5

confirmed.statement: The arm descriptions match the text. ChatGPT-4 worked in two stages: broad suggestions on query, then solution generation on request (Fig. 1 shows it proposing a full idea, 'Emotional Companion Rabbit'). Mr. Ranedeer worked in three stages: preferences and a learning plan, Socratic questioning, then goal-aligned feedback and strategic prompts. Fig. 1 shows the tutor also proposing content in stage 3.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 380), Sect. 3.2.1 and Fig. 1

confirmed.statement: ai_tool.name_model and how_used match the text. Both tools were used through the OpenAI web interface, in a split screen with the AI chat on the left and the solution workspace on the right.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 382), Sect. 3.4.3; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Fig. 3

confirmed.statement: preregistered = not_stated is right. The chapter mentions no preregistration or registry, only approval by the local ethics committee.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1; full-text search of PDF pp. 1-13

confirmed.statement: The chapter does not say which product went with which task or condition, as the form says. Sect. 3.4.1 names two products with 'e.g.'. Fig. 1 uses a plush bunny in both conditions, and Fig. 3 shows a plush bunny task in the Mr. Ranedeer chat. If products were tied to condition, product would be confounded with condition even under a random order. The form keeps this as an open question.
confirmed.locator: PDF pp. 6-7 (printed pp. 381-382), Sect. 3.4.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 380), Fig. 1; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Fig. 3

confirmed.statement: n_analyzed = 62 in each arm fits the text. No exclusions are reported, and the Table 1 effect sizes equal |Z|/sqrt(62) after rounding (Z of 0.73, 0.31, and 2.39 give r of .09, .04, and .30). This is a checker's calculation. The chapter prints no N with any test.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 384), Table 1; PDF p. 1 (printed p. 376), Abstract; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1

summary: The chapter supports the form's assignment, arms, and ai_tool coding: all 62 students used both GPT-4 tools (standard ChatGPT-4 and the personalized tutor Mr. Ranedeer) to write their own Product Improvement solutions, the order was counterbalanced into two groups of 31, and the only 'random' in the document is the order in which raters saw solutions (PDF pp. 1, 5-7; Fig. 2). Because the chapter never says how students were allocated to the two orders, design_class lab_rct has no textual support, and random assignment to generative-AI conditions (criterion 1) is neither shown nor ruled out.
